Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The Supreme Court is allowing the Trump administration to resume, for now, deportations of migrants
to countries other than their birthplaces.
NPR's Sergio Martinez-Beltran reports the court will hear oral arguments on the case
in December.
The justices' brief order state a lower court order that blocked the third country deportations.
The court's three liberal justices objected.
The administration has said that a country's assurance that it will not engage in persecution
or torture should be enough to deport a non-citizen to a country that's not their own.
Solicitor General John Sauer told the justices third country deportations is "an essential
tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."
The policy has been used to deport tens of thousands of non-citizens to countries in
Africa and Latin America, where their attorneys say the migrants face significant harms.
Sergio Martinez-Beltran, NPR News, Austin, Texas.
As President Trump hosted a group of leading A.I. executives at the White House today,
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was in San Francisco unveiling new products at the company's dev
day event.
From Member Station KQED, Rachel Myro reports, "Outside the event, protesters demanded
OpenAI stop working with the military and ICE.
Inside one product was missing, GPT 6.1.
OpenAI held back its release of the model after tests found the model overstepped its
authority and misreported what it had done.
Instead, Altman pitched dots always on A.I. agents designed to act before you ask."
"It can hugely magnify your ability and expand your potential, working 24/7 to take on things
that you don't want to do, so you can focus on higher-level work."
Back in Washington, D.C., President Trump brushed off calls for new guardrails saying
the industry should regulate itself.
For NPR News, I'm Rachel Myro.
Tomorrow, the U.S. military formally pulls out of Iraq after more than two tumultuous
decades there.
NPR's Jane Arav reports from Baghdad the withdrawal will also mark the end of the anti-ISIS coalition
that the U.S. led since 2014.
At what had been the Joint Military Command Center, Iraqi workers are renovating.
U.S. officers have operated from here since 2014, when Iraq asked the U.S. military to
return to fight the militant group ISIS.
On Wednesday, U.S. commanders and Iraqi leaders will mark the withdrawal of U.S. forces 23
years after the United States invaded Iraq.
"It's a historical day.
We are very proud to reach this day."
That's Iraqi Armed Forces spokesman Sabah Al-Nouman.
At its height during an eight-year-long occupation, the U.S. had 170,000 military personnel in
Iraq.
Jane Arav and NPR News begged Dad.
"The stocks drifted lower on Wall Street today and the S&P 500 fell nearly two-tenths
of a percent."
This is NPR.
Two U.S. Navy aviators ejected while landing their plane on the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower
aircraft carrier off of Virginia's coast.
Both aviators were rescued, six sailors aboard the ship were also injured, the incident happened
after a failure of the arresting gear designed to halt a jet after landing.
The MacArthur Foundation announced this year's recipients of the so-called Genius Grant,
NPR's Chloe Veltman reports it's an eclectic bunch.
A historian who studies racial wage gaps, a forensic anthropologist who repatriates
the remains of migrants along the Texas-Mexico border, and a jazz saxophonist whose live performances
include a chef cooking meals on stage.
Their names are Alora DeRenancourt, Kate Spradley, and Emmanuel Wilkins, respectively, and they
are among the 20 recipients of the MacArthur Foundation's no-strings-attached $800,000
MacArthur Fellowship Grants for 2026.
Wilkins, who recently performed an NPR Tiny Desk concert, likened reinterpreting the music
of jazz greats like John Coltrane to cooking in a recent interview with the arts presenter
SF Jazz.
"We're dealing with recipes that you might have gotten from your mother's mother, your
mother's mother's mother."
The MacArthur Fellowship program is now in its 45th year.
Chloe Veltman, NPR News.
The MacArthur Foundation is a financial supporter of NPR.
Researchers discovered a new penguin species living on the Kergulin Islands in the Indian
Ocean about 1,200 miles north of Antarctica.
It's the first new penguin species identified in over 100 years, with the last being the
Northern Rockhopper penguin in 1921.
This is NPR News.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman unveils new AI agent products at dev day event in San Francisco
